🚀 How to Blow Up on YouTube

Before we dive in. It's worth keeping in mind what is universally true for growing a YouTube channel in 2026.

⭐ Our north star
We only make videos that are built and pre-validated for YouTube — before we film.

Ideas generally fall into two buckets:

Pre-validated, YouTube-native ideas
30x+

Reverse-engineered before a video is shot

These are ideas we reverse-engineer from formats already proven to work (on this channel, or via outlier research on other channels) before a video is shot. Built for the platform from the title, thumbnail and hook first.

Repurposed ideas
1.5x

Made for another purpose, adapted after the fact

Content created for another purpose (stage talks, masterclasses, summits, newsletter articles) that we then try to make work on YouTube after the fact.

The performance gap between the two is significant - even with small data from Vishen's current channel. Pre-validated content is hitting up to 30x+, while repurposed ideas barely go past 1.5x.

YouTube First
Repurposed

Why this is our north star:

  • When we back the right ideas from day one → results come faster, less wheel-spinning, and the growth curve we've already started to see compounds more quickly.
    • YouTube videos get posted once per week. Assuming perfect conditions and no gaps in filming. That's a long feedback cycle. 4 videos per month. 52 videos per year. Each one is a "shot on target" with the YouTube algorithm.
    • Learning? After a baseline level of consistency, video idea quality becomes a critical lever for growth.
  • Every decision below, I'd love to keep this principle in mind as it will guide us to a better, healthier YouTube Strategy.
  • These decisions are designed to give you all the information to understand the trade-offs so you know exactly what to expect.

🎙️ The Podcast Decision

Vishen wants to launch a podcast called Scaling Wisdom. The format is recurring solo videos plus occasional guests. The value proposition is aligned to personal and professional growth, scaling impact through influence, mastery and entrepreneurship. It is not a place to talk about Vishen's other value propositions like spirituality and meditation. There are 2 decisions which sit inside this: where does this go, and which guests to feature.

Decision 1 of 5

How do we run Scaling Wisdom?

The podcast is an entirely different format to the talking head. It's a longer run time (1hr+), between 2 people, with a dialogue structure. Episodes which perform best usually skew towards the guest choice. Talking head videos are slightly shorter (20-35 mins), it's solo-led, with a clear hook and value proposition and payoff. These are 2 different sets of expectations for the viewer.

A
Put it on @vishen → solo episodes + some with occasional guests Agreed

The occasional video gets shared here and we vet heavily for guest calibre and value proposition. Key risk is that for every one podcast episode that gets made, it's one less talking head video which can hurt growth if we aren't seeing solid growth. Look at the comparison above which has played out in a similar way already.

B
A full, longer-form podcast format on a dedicated channel

If you want to build a strong consistent podcast, then you'll need a dedicated channel as the viewing behaviour is different to the viewing behaviour of a talking head style video - it's not as framework based or active, it's lean-back content that's lengthier and more story driven so you end up getting a split audience putting them on one channel - it will be so much harder to grow (& very very slow) as you'll be making content for two different audiences.

📌 What's been agreed

Scaling Wisdom folds into @Vishen — no separate channel.

Is this still the right call? We're doing as we're told. But also pointing out the key risks here with the decision as it relates to this current channel.

So far:

  • Proposed cadence: 1-2 episodes a month, so it doesn't hurt talking head split.
  • Guests are occasional, not weekly = there's room to keep it on @Vishen.
  • A weekly, 90-min+ guest show would not fit @Vishen's current viewing behaviour.

Trade-offs

  • ✅ One channel, one brand. Momentum compounds on a channel that's already working.
  • ⚠️ Off-topic or over-long guest episodes muddy the algorithm's read of the channel.
  • 🎨 Branding must stay synonymous with @Vishen - not a separate-looking brand. Podcast risk is that Scaling Wisdom has its own standalone IP.

Our suggestion

Run it as YouTube-first episodes → not a long-form podcast.

1. Title and thumbnail is YouTube-first. 2. We prepare a dedicated hook that's recorded separately to the episode. 3. Body of the video is a splice between Vishen explaining each lesson, then splicing a piece of dialogue from the actual episode, then back to Vishen again. Example of this podcast meets talking head format here.

Two guests/month, topics tied to scaling / foundership (not spirituality).

Method: We did a full-name YouTube search per guest. Pulled the top 3 podcast/interview appearances on other channels (excluding own-channel videos, TEDx talks, keynotes and motivational edits). Rows sorted by median descending views as a proxy for what they could get for us.

What we found. Daniel Priestley is the strongest pull for views. He already operates in the founder/business space which aligns well. The rest sit outside that niche (wellness, breathwork, relationships, energy work, dating), so steering their conversation toward founders or in the space we are trying to own with @Vishen, might come across as forced rather than credible authority they're already known/liked/trusted for.

What that means. Off-niche guests don't really cross-pollinate audiences, their followers aren't there for founder/AI content, so it won't get pushed into that world by YouTube, and it can muddy the algorithm's read on what the channel is about.

Our suggestion

Move forward with Daniel Priestley in London. He's the one guest where this genuinely works.

Make a clear decision on the podcast play overall. If it makes less sense then we can turn this "episode" into a dedicated talking head collaboration video which could stand to get stronger views since his audience is at 200,000 subscribers now.

If you want to bring the others in too, we'd only recommend it as a fully-owned, YouTube-first format we control start to finish, more like a masterclass (think Alex Hormozi's masterclass videos), not a podcast.

That does mean proper scripting throughout, so it's a longer, more involved production than a straight podcast recording. Alex Hormozi video style here.

Or, hold the wider podcast idea until Vishen's channel has built more authority of its own.

Hormozi built his name and following through his own talking-head content first, then introduced talks and masterclasses once that authority existed. That sequencing tends to land better than doing it too early.

🎬 Romania Talk

In motion Option B.. this is already filmed (a purpose-shot intro to bolt onto the talk). This section documents the trade-offs anyway.

Decision 3 of 5

Do we put the Romania stage talk onto the new channel?

A
Rebuild the talk as a dedicated YouTube video, reverse-engineered for the platform Our recommendation

This is the best way to make sure this video lands. There are very few examples of repurposed talks with a YouTube title and thumbnail performing well. But if we reverse engineered why this talk landed so well with a live audience, we can have Vishen deliver this straight to camera instead.

B
Bolt a purpose-shot YouTube intro/hook onto the front of the existing talk Currently being filmed

The hook is the most important part of a YouTube video so if we can properly set expectations with the viewer we are less likely to see a sharp drop-off.

C
Keep the talk in its original form and place it on a channel where the long keynote format already fits

There are very few examples of repurposed talks with a YouTube title and thumbnail performing well. It can be a little click bait and mismatch against viewer expectations. Could also hurt the channel's overall positioning.

What research tells us

  • We've seen the below pattern hold true across channels (not just Vishen's): content built specifically for YouTube consistently outperforms content that wasn't.
  • Same creator, same channel: content made for YouTube is hitting 30x+, content that wasn't is barely doing 1.5x. It's the format it was built for that decides performance which is why we'd like to stick to a consistent format.
YouTube-validated ideas
Repurposed ideas from newsletter
  • The talk falls into that second bucket, it wasn't built for YouTube, so by that same logic we'd expect it to underperform the same way.
  • On top of that, the pacing works against it too: full keynote structure, stage audio, no cuts or pattern breaks, doesn't match the fast-hook, tightly edited style that's been driving Vishen's growth.
  • Once viewers hit that shift mid-video, watch time drops, and that can drag down how YouTube treats the rest of the channel too.
✅ Our recommendation

Option A → Rebuild it natively for YouTube. A bit more production time, but genuinely what we'd recommend, and the one that fits the north star.

📺 Legacy YouTube Channel Consolidation

There are three channels in play, and part of what we need to agree is the role each one takes from here. The way we understand it:

The one to protect

@Vishen (the new channel)

The founder-led entrepreneurship-and-influence channel we launched and are actively growing. Past 17,500 subscribers, with a video going viral (~70k views in two weeks). This is the one that's working, and the one we want to protect.

Old personal channel

Vishen Lakhiani

18-year-old account with mixed history of value propositions and a stale audience. It shows signs of boosted (paid) engagement, and its best-performing videos are spirituality-led — which is why it's the wrong home for the new entrepreneurship focus.

Brand channel

Mindvalley

2M+ subscribers, but a largely dormant audience built over years of talks and paid promotion. The brief we've been given is to make it feel more organic and less like an ad channel. But we need to weigh this against hurting the growth and brand equity of the new channel.

Decision 4 of 5

What do we do with the old channel and its back catalogue now that @Vishen is the home?

A
Unlist the strongest old videos and remake them natively on @Vishen — better than the originals Our recommendation

These videos can be updated and improved now we have data around what made them work so well in the first place.

B
Delete them from Vishen Lakhiani and re-upload to @Vishen, but only after confirming the safe waiting period with YouTube's partner manager

Note: we heard back from partner manager and it's not clear if this is possible, Glen is following up with a new team. It's highly risky because it could be deemed as bot behaviour or spam activity which can inadvertently blacklist the channel. This isn't a hypothetical scenario as we've seen it happen before.

C
Unlist the old videos and repurpose them for social media or email content

What we found

  • We've agreed not to mash the two channels into one — @Vishen is the new account and stays the focus.
  • The risk with straight re-uploading: if YouTube sees an identical title, thumbnail, description, transcript or metadata, it can trigger spam/bot filters and penalise the new channel — the last thing we want on an account that's finally earning organic traction.

Our suggestion. Remaking the best of them natively on @Vishen (Option A) captures the value without the re-upload risk — and we can make them stronger the second time. If Vishen wants to move the originals directly, we confirm the safe approach with the partner manager first rather than guessing.

Decision 5 of 5

Should @Vishen videos be collaborated with the Mindvalley YouTube channel?

A
Case-by-case. Collab only where there's genuine audience or topic crossover Our recommendation

e.g. the female-leadership video, where Mindvalley's audience skews female.

B
Collab on all organic @Vishen videos, as originally requested, to feed the Mindvalley channel

This can hurt the growth of the @Vishen channel if it starts to feel like a brand collaboration or a weak value proposition cross over.

C
Don't collab; keep the channels separate

What we found

  • The goal behind the request is sound: Mindvalley wants to look like a value-driven channel rather than a sales one, and collabs surface organic @Vishen content there.
  • The trade-off cuts the other way, though: collaborating with a brand/business account marginally helps Mindvalley's perception, but it makes @Vishen — a personal-brand, founder-led channel — start to look like an advert for Mindvalley. That's the opposite of what makes this channel work.
  • The audience Mindvalley would send is largely dormant, so the upside for @Vishen is limited even where crossover exists.
  • Collaborating with Vishen Lakhiani (a genuine personal-brand channel) is far lower-risk than collaborating with the Mindvalley brand account.
  • Interim step already in place: an unlisted playlist of @Vishen's videos now sits in the top section of the Mindvalley homepage — so Mindvalley gets organic-looking content without a formal collab diluting @Vishen.

Our suggestion. Keep it case-by-case (Option A): collab only where the audiences or topic genuinely overlap, lean on the Vishen Lakhiani channel over the Mindvalley brand account where we can, and use the homepage playlist to satisfy the "make Mindvalley feel organic" goal in the meantime. Long-term the Mindvalley channel needs its own dedicated strategy to have a strong organic audience and we can't optimize a YouTube Strategy on @vishen for 2 separate goals. Typically you will fail at achieving either when taking a middle ground.

Close. These are all of the active decisions in a nutshell. Where possible we have given formal recommendations on what we would do if we were in service of the best organic results possible for the channel.
